Title: Your T-Stop Wheels Should Graze, Not Dig
Description: The T-stop fails for one reason more than any other: too much pressure. Shift your weight onto the supporting leg to lighten the other, then set the free skate down behind it and let the wheels drag across the surface instead of biting into it. Press harder and you get a jolt, and the jolt is what throws you off. Two wheels down or four, it makes no difference. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: t-stop, roller skate braking, quad skating, how to stop on skates

Title: On Quads, the Toe Stop Goes Down at a Quarter Turn
Description: This one is quad-only, and it matters: your toe stop goes down at a quarter turn, knee open, never square to the front. Square on, it chatters and catches; turned a quarter, it sits. And the skater behind this site is clear on what it is for: not braking. A toe stop is a fixed point that does not roll, there to hold still, pivot and push off. Inline skaters, your brake sits at the back and none of this transfers. From Najete Kada. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: toe stop, quad skates, quad skate toe stop uses, quad technique

Title: Skating Backwards, Your Weight Still Goes Forward
Description: Everyone leans back the first time, and everyone falls. Rolling backwards keeps the pressure on the front of your skates, exactly as it does going forwards, and that is the part nobody expects. Start in an inverted V with your toes together, and walk backwards by lifting one skate then the other before you let yourself roll. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Backwards Skating Starts at Your Knees
Description: The hardest part of going backwards has nothing to do with your feet. Your knees have to stay pressed together, and holding them there is hard work, which is why most people give up on the position before they give up on the movement. Toes together, knees squeezed, and the skates roll where you want them. Let the knees drift apart and the whole thing falls open. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: skating backwards, knee position skating, quad skating, skating drills

Title: Find Your Weight by Putting Your Hands on Your Navel
Description: A simple way to feel where your weight actually sits: put both hands on your navel and move it over one skate. Skate, navel, upper body in one line, and that is the whole check. It works for transitions, for rolling on one foot, for anything that asks you to load a single leg. Looking down at your feet tells you nothing. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. Title: Bring Your Skates Side by Side Before You Transfer
Description: The single most important habit for rolling on one foot happens before the interesting part. Bring both skates level with each other, set the returning skate down underneath your hips, and only then move your weight across. Put it down anywhere else and the transfer fights you. Do it in the right order and one-foot rolling stops being a balance trick. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: one foot skating, weight transfer, quad skating, skating technique

Title: The Skating Stride Is Just a Weight Transfer, Sped Up
Description: Nobody teaches the stride as a separate skill, because it is not one. Roll on one foot, bring the skates level, transfer, roll on the other, then do the same thing faster. That is the stride. Knowing the order matters, because it means the fix for a clumsy stride is never more speed. It is going back to the slow transfer and cleaning it up. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: skating stride, roller skating technique, quad skating, learn to skate

Title: A Good Fall Is a Descent, Not a Drop
Description: You are not trying to avoid the fall. You are trying to slow it down. From the safety position, knees bent and hands resting on your knees, lower yourself into a squat until you touch the floor, put your hands down, then stretch your legs out in front of you. Three movements, practised slowly, in full gear, on a soft floor and never alone. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: how to fall skating, safety position, quad skating, roller skate safety

Title: Getting Up: Turn Over, One Knee, One Skate
Description: Getting back up has a shape, and flailing is not it. Roll over onto your knees, plant one skate flat on the floor in front of you, then push up off that leg while your hands press down on the knee to help. It is the position a knight takes to kneel. Slow, repeatable, and it works when you are tired, which is exactly when you will need it. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: how to get up skating, roller skate falls, quad skating, beginner skating

Title: The Roller Dance Steps, Named
Description: Every roller dance step you have watched has a name, and they all count in four. Bounce. Dribble, where one leg passes the other. Shuffle, crossing on the toes. Catwalk. Downtown, which is cross in front, cross behind, then double it. And Moonwalk: right skate on its toe, left skate on the stop, press hard into the stop and drag the rolling skate backwards. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. Illustration generated with AI.
